metadata.narrative: I'm helping a city council delegation prepare for meetings in Copenhagen and Stockholm about immigration policy. Denmark and Sweden both have strong welfare states, but seem to have moved in different ways since the 2015 refugee influx. How should we understand the tradeoffs between Denmark's harder deterrence and parallel society approach and Sweden's earlier welcoming model followed by a tougher political turn? What should local officials pay attention to on asylum, housing segregation, labor-market integration, public backlash, and risks of importing either model into our own city?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Denmark and Sweden entered 2015 as archetypes of generous Nordic welfare states, yet the scale of arrivals split them onto sharply different paths that a city delegation should treat as two distinct policy experiments rather than a simple "tough versus soft" binary.

On asylum, Denmark moved fastest and hardest: in 2019 its prime minister declared a goal of "zero asylum seekers," and Denmark became the first EU country to revoke residency permits for Syrian refugees once it judged parts of Syria safe enough to return to.

Copenhagen amended its migration rules roughly seventy times between 2015 and 2018 and in 2015 passed a law authorizing the seizure of asylum seekers' valuables alongside benefit cuts of up to 50 percent, explicitly framed as making Denmark less attractive than Sweden.
UNHCR data show Denmark granted protection to just 2,365 people in 2017 against Sweden's 26,775, and separate Danish reporting put 2016 grants at only about 7,400.

Sweden's story reversed direction rather than starting restrictive: its prime minister opened 2015 promising a Europe "open and helpful," then closed the border that same autumn, made temporary permits the default, and by 2021 had added a "safe country" list for fast-track denials.
That trajectory continued after the 2022 election, when the Tidö Agreement between the Moderate-led coalition and the Sweden Democrats cut the annual refugee quota from 5,000 to 900.
Housing policy is where Denmark's deterrence logic becomes most visible and contested.
A 1986 dispersal act spread refugees across counties, and a 1998 Integration Act tied benefits and housing to a designated municipality to prevent self-directed clustering.

The 2018 "ghetto law," rebranded in 2021 as targeting "parallel societies," designates areas as ghettos when over half of residents are non-Western and two of four socioeconomic criteria are met, triggering demolitions, doubled sentences, whole-family eviction if a child is convicted of a crime, day-care caps of 30 percent, and a $1.45 billion redevelopment budget, and it now faces a discrimination challenge before the EU Court of Justice.

Fieldwork in Trigeparken outside Aarhus found falling crime and improving school attainment behind the "ghetto" label, suggesting stigmatization outpaces reality and structural, not ethnic, factors drive most residents' problems.

Sweden's segregation grew differently, as an unintended consequence of the 1960s-70s Miljonprogram public-housing build-out, whose "concrete suburbs" absorbed refugee resettlement and became durably identified with immigrant populations.

That segregation became visible through unrest: a 2008 dispute over mosque premises in Malmö's Rosengård escalated into weeks of rioting with pipe bombs, and 2013 riots across Stockholm suburbs followed a police shooting, reflecting economic and housing conditions more than immigration itself.
Labor-market outcomes complicate any simple verdict.

Denmark's "Start Aid" benefit cuts, begun in 2002 to push refugees into work, produced only a brief early bump before nine-to-ten-year outcomes converged to near zero, while child poverty in immigrant households rose from about 42,500 to 64,500 poor children between 2016 and 2017.
Yet other Danish reporting points to a 60 percent rise in employment among newly arrived refugees, showing integration trends can diverge from harsh political rhetoric.

Sweden shows the widest native-foreign employment gap among 31 OECD countries in 2011, roughly 76.6 percent versus 62.6 percent, but part of that reflects Sweden's unusually high native female labor participation rather than uniquely poor immigrant outcomes.

Activity rates are structurally lower for refugees than labor migrants, Swedish proficiency alone raised employment odds by about ten points, and foreign-born unemployment rose from 1.7 to 16.2 percent between 1970 and 2010 as migration shifted toward humanitarian arrivals.
Public backlash followed related but distinct arcs.

Denmark's Danish People's Party became parliament's second-largest party in 2015 on an anti-immigration platform, while Sweden's Sweden Democrats crossed the parliamentary threshold in 2010 before winning 20.5 percent of the vote in 2022 and becoming kingmaker under the Tidö Agreement.

Danish demographers and historians have supplied intellectual rationale for restriction, citing rising non-Western population share, an estimated annual net fiscal cost of 15-20 billion DKK, and cultural friction over gender norms and secularism.

Danish crime data show non-Western descendants over-represented in convictions, but Danes confess to charges twice as often as immigrants, crime types differ by group, and documented ethnic profiling in stop-and-search inflates arrest statistics independent of actual offending.

Sweden's gang-violence crisis, with shootings running several times the European average, led even its center-right prime minister to attribute violence primarily to segregation rather than immigration, while noting gangs recruit children as young as fifteen to exploit sentencing loopholes.

Some Swedish politicians have pointed to Denmark's harsher sentencing and stop-and-search zones as a model credited with cutting gang membership by roughly a third over a decade, showing the two countries' policies already influence each other.
For a city council weighing what to import, the clearest caution is against treating either toolkit as a package deal.
Denmark's ethnicity-linked area designations achieved political signaling but face live legal challenge and case evidence that stigma outpaced actual conditions.

Its benefit-conditionality approach shows a checkable failure mode of minimal long-run employment gains paired with higher child poverty, even as broader refugee employment reportedly improved over time.
Sweden's experience warns that rapid, concentrated placement without matching language and employment investment can produce durable segregation and unrest years later.

Officials should treat crime and employment statistics skeptically until disaggregated, since headline gaps can reflect comparison baselines, confession and policing patterns, or native-population composition rather than newcomer failure.

Practically, this favors pairing any deterrence measures with independent stigma monitoring, avoiding ethnicity-based area thresholds given their legal exposure, and prioritizing dispersed housing and employment-service integration over benefit cuts or demolition as the more defensible levers for a city.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Copenhagen amended its migration rules roughly seventy times between 2015 and 2018, cut refugee aid, and in 2015 passed a law authorizing the seizure of asylum seekers' valuables alongside benefit cuts of up to 50 percent, explicitly framed as making Denmark less attractive than Sweden.
The numbers show the deterrence worked in volume terms: Denmark granted protection to only 2,365 people in 2017, compared with nearly 28,000 in Sweden the same year.
Sweden's asylum story reversed direction rather than starting restrictive: its prime minister opened 2015 promising a Europe "open and helpful," then closed the border that same autumn, made temporary residence permits the default, and by June 2021 had passed a harsher law introducing a "safe country" list for fast-track denials.
That trajectory continued after the 2022 election, when the Tidö Agreement between the Moderate-led coalition and the Sweden Democrats cut the annual refugee resettlement quota from 5,000 to just 900.

Housing policy is where Denmark's deterrence logic becomes most visible and most contested.
Denmark's spatial approach has deep roots: a 1986 dispersal act geographically spread refugees across counties, and a 1998 Integration Act tied benefits and housing assignment to a designated municipality specifically to prevent self-directed clustering.
The 2018 "ghetto law," rebranded in 2021 as targeting "parallel societies," designates areas as ghettos when over half of residents are non-Western and two of four socioeconomic criteria are met, triggering demolitions, day-care enrollment caps of 30 percent for neighborhood children, and a $1.45 billion redevelopment budget through 2026, and it is now the subject of a discrimination challenge before the European Court of Justice.
Fieldwork in one such area, Trigeparken outside Aarhus, found falling crime and improving school attainment behind the "ghetto" label, suggesting the designation stigmatizes communities without matching lived reality and that housing-cost and structural factors, not ethnicity itself, drive most residents' problems.
Sweden's segregation grew differently, as an unintended consequence of the 1960s-70s Miljonprogram public-housing build-out, whose "concrete suburbs" absorbed successive waves of refugee resettlement and became durably identified with immigrant populations.
That segregation became visible through unrest: a 2008 dispute over mosque premises in Malmö's Rosengård district escalated into weeks of rioting with pipe bombs, and 2013 riots across Stockholm suburbs followed a police shooting, reflecting economic and housing conditions more than immigration flows or integration-program failure as such.

Labor-market outcomes complicate any simple verdict on either country's approach.
Denmark's "Start Aid" benefit reductions, begun in 2002 to push refugees into work, produced only a brief early employment bump before nine-to-ten-year outcomes converged to near zero, while child poverty in immigrant and vulnerable households rose sharply, from about 42,500 poor children in 2016 to 64,500 in 2017.
Sweden shows a persistent employment gap that OECD data ranked the widest among 31 countries in 2011, at roughly 76.6 percent native employment versus 62.6 percent foreign-born, but part of that gap reflects Sweden's unusually high native female labor-force participation rather than uniquely poor immigrant outcomes, a nuance city officials should not skip past.
Underlying mechanisms matter for local design: activity rates are structurally lower for refugees and family migrants than for labor migrants, Swedish-language proficiency alone raised employment odds by about ten percentage points, and foreign-born unemployment in Sweden rose from 1.7 to 16.2 percent between 1970 and 2010 as the composition of migration shifted from labor recruitment toward humanitarian arrivals.

Public backlash followed similar but not identical arcs in both countries.
Denmark's Danish People's Party became parliament's second-largest party in 2015 on an anti-immigration platform, while Sweden's Sweden Democrats crossed the parliamentary threshold in 2010, were long shunned by mainstream parties, but by 2022 won 20.5 percent of the vote and became kingmaker for the Kristersson government under the Tidö Agreement.

answer.text: Denmark and Sweden entered 2015 as archetypes of generous Nordic welfare states, yet the scale of arrivals split them onto sharply different paths that a city delegation should treat as two distinct policy experiments rather than a simple "tough versus soft" binary.

On asylum, Denmark moved fastest and hardest: in 2019 its prime minister declared a goal of "zero asylum seekers," and Denmark became the first EU country to revoke residency permits for Syrian refugees once it judged parts of Syria safe enough to return to.

Copenhagen amended its migration rules roughly seventy times between 2015 and 2018 and in 2015 passed a law authorizing the seizure of asylum seekers' valuables alongside benefit cuts of up to 50 percent, explicitly framed as making Denmark less attractive than Sweden.
UNHCR data show Denmark granted protection to just 2,365 people in 2017 against Sweden's 26,775, and separate Danish reporting put 2016 grants at only about 7,400.

Sweden's story reversed direction rather than starting restrictive: its prime minister opened 2015 promising a Europe "open and helpful," then closed the border that same autumn, made temporary permits the default, and by 2021 had added a "safe country" list for fast-track denials.
That trajectory continued after the 2022 election, when the Tidö Agreement between the Moderate-led coalition and the Sweden Democrats cut the annual refugee quota from 5,000 to 900.
Housing policy is where Denmark's deterrence logic becomes most visible and contested.
A 1986 dispersal act spread refugees across counties, and a 1998 Integration Act tied benefits and housing to a designated municipality to prevent self-directed clustering.

The 2018 "ghetto law," rebranded in 2021 as targeting "parallel societies," designates areas as ghettos when over half of residents are non-Western and two of four socioeconomic criteria are met, triggering demolitions, doubled sentences, whole-family eviction if a child is convicted of a crime, day-care caps of 30 percent, and a $1.45 billion redevelopment budget, and it now faces a discrimination challenge before the EU Court of Justice.

Fieldwork in Trigeparken outside Aarhus found falling crime and improving school attainment behind the "ghetto" label, suggesting stigmatization outpaces reality and structural, not ethnic, factors drive most residents' problems.

Sweden's segregation grew differently, as an unintended consequence of the 1960s-70s Miljonprogram public-housing build-out, whose "concrete suburbs" absorbed refugee resettlement and became durably identified with immigrant populations.

That segregation became visible through unrest: a 2008 dispute over mosque premises in Malmö's Rosengård escalated into weeks of rioting with pipe bombs, and 2013 riots across Stockholm suburbs followed a police shooting, reflecting economic and housing conditions more than immigration itself.
Labor-market outcomes complicate any simple verdict.

Denmark's "Start Aid" benefit cuts, begun in 2002 to push refugees into work, produced only a brief early bump before nine-to-ten-year outcomes converged to near zero, while child poverty in immigrant households rose from about 42,500 to 64,500 poor children between 2016 and 2017.
Yet other Danish reporting points to a 60 percent rise in employment among newly arrived refugees, showing integration trends can diverge from harsh political rhetoric.

Sweden shows the widest native-foreign employment gap among 31 OECD countries in 2011, roughly 76.6 percent versus 62.6 percent, but part of that reflects Sweden's unusually high native female labor participation rather than uniquely poor immigrant outcomes.

Activity rates are structurally lower for refugees than labor migrants, Swedish proficiency alone raised employment odds by about ten points, and foreign-born unemployment rose from 1.7 to 16.2 percent between 1970 and 2010 as migration shifted toward humanitarian arrivals.
Public backlash followed related but distinct arcs.

Denmark's Danish People's Party became parliament's second-largest party in 2015 on an anti-immigration platform, while Sweden's Sweden Democrats crossed the parliamentary threshold in 2010 before winning 20.5 percent of the vote in 2022 and becoming kingmaker under the Tidö Agreement.

Danish demographers and historians have supplied intellectual rationale for restriction, citing rising non-Western population share, an estimated annual net fiscal cost of 15-20 billion DKK, and cultural friction over gender norms and secularism.

Danish crime data show non-Western descendants over-represented in convictions, but Danes confess to charges twice as often as immigrants, crime types differ by group, and documented ethnic profiling in stop-and-search inflates arrest statistics independent of actual offending.

Sweden's gang-violence crisis, with shootings running several times the European average, led even its center-right prime minister to attribute violence primarily to segregation rather than immigration, while noting gangs recruit children as young as fifteen to exploit sentencing loopholes.

Some Swedish politicians have pointed to Denmark's harsher sentencing and stop-and-search zones as a model credited with cutting gang membership by roughly a third over a decade, showing the two countries' policies already influence each other.
For a city council weighing what to import, the clearest caution is against treating either toolkit as a package deal.
Denmark's ethnicity-linked area designations achieved political signaling but face live legal challenge and case evidence that stigma outpaced actual conditions.

Its benefit-conditionality approach shows a checkable failure mode of minimal long-run employment gains paired with higher child poverty, even as broader refugee employment reportedly improved over time.
Sweden's experience warns that rapid, concentrated placement without matching language and employment investment can produce durable segregation and unrest years later.

Officials should treat crime and employment statistics skeptically until disaggregated, since headline gaps can reflect comparison baselines, confession and policing patterns, or native-population composition rather than newcomer failure.

Practically, this favors pairing any deterrence measures with independent stigma monitoring, avoiding ethnicity-based area thresholds given their legal exposure, and prioritizing dispersed housing and employment-service integration over benefit cuts or demolition as the more defensible levers for a city.
